name: Fisetin

lead: Fisetin is a flavonol found in strawberries, apples and onions, sold as a supplement and discussed as a candidate senolytic, a compound that selectively clears senescent cells.
It gained attention after mouse studies reported extended health and lifespan. Human data are limited to early or ongoing trials, and no appearance benefit has been demonstrated.

paras: In cell and mouse studies fisetin reduced senescent-cell burden and inflammatory signaling, possibly via pathways involving PI3K/AKT and mTOR modulation, along with antioxidant effects.
Human safety data at the doses discussed online are sparse. Possible interactions with drugs are not well characterized. Legal as a supplement, but not an approved therapy for any condition.

lead: Fisetin (3,3',4',7-tetrahydroxyflavone) is a plant flavonol in the polyphenol family. It occurs as a yellow pigment in fruits and vegetables such as strawberries, apples, persimmons, onions and cucumbers, and its chemical formula was first described by the Austrian chemist Josef Herzig in 1891.[1] It is sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement and is discussed in longevity communities as a candidate senolytic, a compound proposed to selectively clear senescent cells.[2][3]

Interest rose after a 2018 EBioMedicine paper reported that fisetin acted as a senotherapeutic that extended health and lifespan in mice.[4] Human data remain limited to small or early-phase trials, several of them registered but not yet reporting, and Wikipedia states that there was no clinical evidence of benefit to human health as of 2018.[1] No published human trial has tested fisetin for skin, hair or facial appearance outcomes.

Fisetin is a supplement and not an approved therapy for any condition. Research reviews describe its oral bioavailability as low, and efforts to improve absorption through new formulations are under way.[5][6]
infobox: Strawberries, apples, persimmons, onions, smoke tree
Dietary supplement; no approved medical indication

paras: Fisetin is a flavonol with a 3-hydroxyflavone core; it differs from the related flavonol quercetin by lacking a hydroxyl group at the 5-position, which is why it is sometimes called 5-deoxyquercetin.[7] Grokipedia reports it was first isolated in 1833 from the smoke tree (Rhus cotinus), a source of yellow dye, and that it is found in plant families including Fabaceae, Moraceae and Anacardiaceae, with strawberries often cited as the richest common dietary source.[7] It is poorly soluble in water and sensitive to light and oxidation.[7] Review articles also discuss methods for preparing it at pharmaceutical quality.[8]

Fisetin shares the antioxidant properties of other polyphenols and has been reported in laboratory work to have anti-inflammatory, chemopreventive and neuroprotective activity.[8][9][10] Fisetin and quercetin were among the first agents identified as senolytics, drugs that make senescent cells susceptible to their own pro-apoptotic environment.[11][12] Senescent cells accumulate with age and secrete an inflammatory mixture called the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP); researchers in the field have proposed that clearing them intermittently, a so-called hit-and-run approach, could delay age-related conditions.[11][11]

A 2017 study in Aging reported fisetin alongside BCL-XL inhibitors as new agents targeting senescent cells.[12] Cell studies have also shown flavonoids, including fisetin, to inhibit phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase signalling.[13] Some work describes a dual character, with phenoxyl radicals of flavonoids having prooxidant activity under some conditions.[14]

Fisetin has low oral bioavailability. A 2022 randomised double-blind crossover study in healthy volunteers compared a novel hybrid-hydrogel formulation with unformulated fisetin and reported enhanced bioavailability for the formulated product.[6] Reviews of fisetin as a senotherapeutic say that safety, pharmacokinetics and efficacy still need to be established in humans.[5]

The senolytic hypothesis is supported mainly by cell and animal work. A review of senolytic drugs reports that in preclinical models they delay, prevent or alleviate frailty and diseases of many organ systems, with translation to humans only beginning.[11][11] A 2024 narrative review concluded that fisetin offers a promising strategy for multiple chronic diseases but stressed that more studies are required to establish safety, pharmacokinetics and efficacy.[5] A separate review of senotherapy in oncology lists fisetin with metformin, rapamycin, dasatinib, quercetin and others as agents that eliminate senescent cells in cell cultures and murine models.[3]

Other lab reports include protection against kidney fibrosis in mice via effects on ferroptosis,[15] a mitochondria-targeted fisetin derivative that limited survival of drug-induced senescent breast cancer cells,[16] and in vitro neuroprotection by quercetin-related flavonoids that was limited in vivo by blood-brain barrier passage for quercetin.[10]

Published randomised trials of fisetin are few and mostly outside the senescence field. A double-blind placebo-controlled trial in ischaemic stroke patients examined whether fisetin could extend the treatment window for tissue plasminogen activator.[17] A placebo-controlled, pseudo-randomised crossover trial tested botanical agents including fisetin (from Rhus succedanea) for Gulf War illness.[18] Two 2026 randomised trials in obese men combined fisetin supplementation with interval resistance-aerobic training and measured adipokines such as asprosin and inflammatory markers including Maresin-1.[19][20] The 2022 hybrid-hydrogel study above is a pharmacokinetic trial in healthy people.[6]

Registered trials target ageing biology. ClinicalTrials.gov lists studies of fisetin for reducing systemic senescence (n=82),[21] vascular function in older adults,[22][23] senescence and walking impairment in peripheral artery disease,[24] multimorbidity,[25] healthy ageing,[26] age-related lung decline,[27] carpal tunnel syndrome,[28] mild Alzheimer's disease,[29] and COVID-19 inflammation.[30] Grokipedia reports that Mayo Clinic's AFFIRM frailty trials had no peer-reviewed primary results posted as of late 2026.[7] No clinical studies on appearance outcomes were found.

Fisetin is generally regarded as low hazard in dietary contexts, though direct contact can irritate skin, eyes and airways.[7] Human safety data at the higher doses discussed in longevity communities are limited, and drug interactions have not been well characterised in published trials.[5]

Fisetin is sold as a supplement. On T Nation, contributors list it among mitochondrial and longevity compounds alongside urolithin A, NAD+ and PQQ,[31] mention strawberries as a fisetin source in discussions of dietary phytochemicals,[32] and have run articles calling it a potential next polyphenol supplement comparable to curcumin and attributing to it effects including reduced body fat, blood sugar regulation and UV skin protection in animal work.[33][34] No looksmax.org or Reddit discussion was identified.

lore.intro: Fisetin is discussed mainly in longevity and supplement circles, including on T Nation, as a senolytic or polyphenol supplement; it is not a core looksmaxxing topic.[31][33]

Josef Herzig describes its chemical formula.[1]
